newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OKs two gas-electric mergers, stalls third.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OKs two gas-electric mergers, stalls third.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Wednesday approved the proposed mergers of Long Island Lighting Co. with Brooklyn Union Gas Co., and PG&E Corp. with Valero Natural Gas Co.

However, the commission put a hold on the proposed union of Ohio Edison Co. and Centerior Energy Corp., ordering them either to revise their merger plan or face a hearing to address the agency's concerns about their ability to dominate the Ohio and western Pennsylvania power markets.

The commission cleared Lilco and Brooklyn Union's plan to form a $4 billion company which will combine all of Brooklyn Union's operations and Lilco's natural gas system, non-nuclear power plants and certain other assets, serving 2.2 million customers in three New York City boroughs and Long Island.

The two companies still need approvals from the New York Public Service Commission, the U.S. Justice Department and Nuclear Regulatory Commission before they can close their deal, a Brooklyn Union spokesman said.

Under the plan, New York's Long Island Power Authority will buy Lilco's electric transmission and distribution system and its share of the upstate Nine Mile Point 2 nuclear plant. The authority will take over $3.6 billion of Lilco's $4.5 billion debt, largely tied to the Shoreham nuclear plant, which never opened.

With the commission's approval, PG&E expects to complete the $1.5 billion acquisition of Valero's natural gas and gas liquids pipelines, processing plants and storage facilities by Aug. 1, a company spokesman said.

The purchase marks PG&E's third recent investment in the natural gas industry in Texas, positioning it to become one of the top 10 U.S. gas marketing operations with daily sales of 3.6 billion cubic feet of gas.

While the commission said the New York and PG&E-Valero mergers would not harm competition, it said in contrast that Ohio Edison and Centerior Energy Corp. had understated their market share and their ability to control transmission capacity and limit rival suppliers' access to the grid.

The commission suggested the two electric utilities could avoid an agency hearing by proposing to sell some power plants, allocate some transmission capacity to other suppliers or expand their transmission systems.
It also recommended that the merged company, FirstEnergy Corp., could turn over control of its transmission systems to an independent operator.

"While we are disappointed that the merger could not receive FERC's approval today, we remain confident in the benefits of our merger and our ability to address FERC's concerns," a spokesman for Ohio Edison said.
